Difference: Freud's theory is psychological and hard to test, while Activation Synthesis is based on measurable biological brain activity (1)

practice_questions.text: Describe the aim, procedure and findings of Freud's (1909) case study of Little Hans.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 5 marks:
• Aim: to investigate the unconscious causes of a child's phobia using psychoanalysis (1)
• Procedure: a case study of a five-year-old boy with a phobia of horses; data came from detailed letters and notes sent by Hans's father describing his fears, dreams and behaviour (1-2)
• Findings/conclusion: Freud interpreted the phobia as a displaced, unconscious fear connected to Hans's father, expressed through a substitute object, the horse (1-2)

practice_questions.text: Evaluate Freud's theory of dreaming as an explanation of why we dream.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Gives a detailed, accurate account of Freud's theory (manifest content, latent content, dreamwork) and develops at least three evaluation points (e.g. low testability/validity, subjective interpretation, lack of biological evidence, comparison with Activation Synthesis Theory) with a clear, supported overall judgement.
Secure: Clear account of the theory with two or more developed evaluation points and some judgement of the theory's value.
Developing: Basic description of the theory with limited or undeveloped evaluation points; judgement may be missing or unsupported.
Emerging: Simple or partial description of the theory; evaluation is absent or only asserted without explanation.

practice_questions.text:
Which type of praise focuses on a child's effort and strategies, rather than their fixed ability?
A) Person praise
B) Process praise
C) Trait praise
D) Outcome praise
practice_questions.marks: B) Process praise is correct because it praises effort and strategy rather than fixed ability. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'growth mindset'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise definition covering both the belief that ability can change AND the mechanism (effort, strategy, learning from mistakes) [2 marks].
Secure: A definition covering the belief that ability can change, with some detail [2 marks].
Developing: A partial or vague definition, e.g. 'thinking you can get smarter' [1 mark].
Emerging: No clear definition or confuses with fixed mindset [0 marks].

practice_questions.text: Explain why a child with a fixed mindset might avoid a difficult challenge at school.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that a fixed mindset treats failure as proof of a permanent limit on ability, so challenge feels threatening, with clear reasoning linking belief to behaviour [3 marks].
Secure: Explains that fixed mindset learners avoid challenge because they fear looking incapable, with some reasoning [2 marks].
Developing: States that fixed mindset learners avoid challenge without explaining why [1 mark].
Emerging: Vague or inaccurate description of mindset [0 marks].

practice_questions.text: Compare a fixed mindset with a growth mindset in terms of how a learner responds to failure.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Gives at least one accurate similarity (e.g. both are beliefs about the cause of success or failure) AND one accurate difference (e.g. fixed mindset attributes outcomes to ability while growth mindset attributes them to effort), referring to both mindsets [4 marks].
Secure: One similarity or difference fully explained, with a partial second point [3 marks].
Developing: Only a difference or only a similarity given, undeveloped [2 marks].
Emerging: Describes one mindset only [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Describe the aim, procedure, results and conclusion of Gunderson et al.'s (2013) study into parent praise.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate aim (testing whether parent praise type predicts children's later motivational framework), procedure (naturalistic observation of parent praise to toddlers aged one to three, coded as process or person praise), results (process praise predicted growth mindset five years later; person praise did not) and conclusion (early effort-focused praise helps build a lasting growth mindset), all correctly attributed to Gunderson et al. (2013) [5 marks].
Secure: Most of aim, procedure, results and conclusion present and accurate, with minor omissions [3-4 marks].
Developing: Some accurate detail but missing at least two of aim, procedure, results or conclusion, or attributes the study to the wrong researcher [1-2 marks].
Emerging: Vague or inaccurate reference to the study [0 marks].

practice_questions.text: Evaluate Dweck's Mindset Theory as an explanation of how children respond to challenge, using evidence from Gunderson et al. (2013) to support your evaluation.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced description of the theory and Gunderson's evidence, with at least two elaborated evaluation points (e.g. correlational design limits causal claims; naturalistic observation supports validity; real-world classroom application) each developed with a reason, ending in a supported judgement [7-8 marks].
Secure: Accurate description with at least two evaluation points, though development or judgement may be limited [5-6 marks].
Developing: Description with one or two undeveloped evaluation points and no clear judgement [3-4 marks].
Emerging: Mostly description, little or no evaluation [1-2 marks].

practice_questions.text:
Which type of punishment involves an offender meeting their victim to discuss the harm caused and how to repair it?
A) Prison
B) Community sentencing
C) Restorative justice
D) Token economy
practice_questions.marks: C) Restorative justice [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: A young offenders' institution tracks 40 offenders who complete an anger-management programme. After one year, 6 of them have reoffended. Calculate the percentage of offenders from this group who did NOT reoffend. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Working: 40 − 6 = 34 offenders did not reoffend; 34 ÷ 40 × 100 = 85%
[1 mark for correct method/working; 1 mark for correct final answer of 85% with % included]

practice_questions.text: Explain why token economy programmes may reduce offending behaviour within an institution.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that tokens act as secondary reinforcers for operant conditioning, with clear reasoning linking reinforcement to repeated good behaviour and reduced rule-breaking.
Secure: Explains that offenders earn tokens for good behaviour which can be exchanged for rewards, with some reasoning about why this encourages behaviour change.
Developing: Describes token economies with limited or unclear reasoning about why behaviour changes.
Emerging: Vague or generic reference to rewards with little explanation.

practice_questions.text: Compare prison and community sentencing as ways of dealing with offenders.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Gives a developed similarity (e.g. both aim to reduce reoffending/punish crime) AND a developed difference (e.g. prison removes the offender from society while community sentencing allows them to remain in the community), referring to both punishments throughout.
Secure: Gives at least one similarity and one difference, referring to both punishments, with some development.
Developing: Gives only a similarity or only a difference, or refers mainly to one punishment.
Emerging: Vague or undeveloped comparison with little reference to both punishments.

practice_questions.text: Describe the aim, procedure and findings of Charlton et al.'s (2000) study of children's playground behaviour on St Helena.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurately describes the aim (testing effects of television on children's behaviour), procedure (naturalistic observation of playground behaviour on St Helena before/after TV introduced in 1995, over five years, using video recordings/checklists) and findings (little change in anti-social behaviour; pro-social behaviour remained common), all correctly attributed.
Secure: Describes most of aim, procedure and findings accurately with minor omissions or imprecision.
Developing: Gives a partial or generalised account, missing key details such as St Helena or the five-year naturalistic design.
Emerging: Very limited or inaccurate description, or confuses this study with another named study.

practice_questions.text: 'Restorative justice is the most effective way to reduce reoffending among young offenders.' Assess this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Considers strengths of restorative justice (e.g. builds empathy/responsibility, gives victims a voice) AND weaknesses (e.g. depends on victim's willingness, unsuitable for serious crimes), compares against at least one alternative (prison, community sentencing or a treatment), and reaches a supported, balanced judgement.
Secure: Gives some strengths and weaknesses of restorative justice with brief comparison to an alternative, reaching a judgement with some support.
Developing: Describes restorative justice with limited evaluation or comparison; judgement is asserted rather than supported.
Emerging: Simple, one-sided or undeveloped response with little evaluation or no clear judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes a cardinal trait in Allport's (1936) theory?
A) A trait that only appears in certain situations
B) A single dominant trait that shapes almost everything a person does
C) A score on one of Cattell's sixteen personality factors
D) A trait shared equally by everyone in a population
practice_questions.marks: B) A single dominant trait that shapes almost everything a person does [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term '16PF'.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks:
• 1 mark for identifying it as Cattell's (1946) personality questionnaire/scale
• 1 mark for stating it measures personality across sixteen trait dimensions/factors, identified using factor analysis

practice_questions.text: Compare Allport's (1936) trait theory with Cattell's (1946) 16PF as ways of measuring personality.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Must refer to both theories and include at least one similarity and one difference, e.g.:
• Similarity: both assume personality is made up of measurable traits rather than fixed types (1-2 marks)
• Difference: Allport organised traits into three levels of importance (cardinal, central, secondary) based on case study/judgement, whereas Cattell used the statistical technique of factor analysis to identify sixteen trait dimensions measured by a standardised questionnaire (1-2 marks)
• Credit any other accurate similarity/difference, e.g. both can be criticised for reductionism, or Cattell's approach produces numerical scores while Allport's does not

practice_questions.text: Describe the aim, procedure and findings of Van Houtte and Jarvis's (1995) study into the role of pets in preadolescent psychosocial development.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 5 marks for accurate detail, e.g.:
• Aim: to investigate whether owning a pet is linked to healthy psychosocial development in preadolescents (self-esteem, self-concept and autonomy) (1 mark)
• Procedure: 130 children aged 8–13 in a matched-pairs design, pairing pet owners with similar non-owners; questionnaires measured autonomy, self-concept, self-esteem and attachment to animals (1-2 marks)
• Findings: pet ownership (not attachment strength) was linked to higher self-esteem, self-concept and autonomy, with the strongest effect in older children around 10–11 (1-2 marks)

practice_questions.text: Amara is 11 years old and has owned a rabbit since she was six years old. Using Van Houtte and Jarvis's (1995) findings, explain what psychologists might predict about Amara's self-esteem.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks for a developed, contextualised explanation, e.g.:
• Identifies that Amara is a pet owner, and an older child close to adolescence (1-2 marks)
• Applies Van Houtte and Jarvis's finding that pet ownership, especially in older children, was linked to higher self-esteem, self-concept and autonomy (1-2 marks)
• Explains that because Amara owns a pet and is around the age where the effect was strongest, psychologists might predict she would show relatively high self-esteem and autonomy (1-2 marks)
• Answer must explicitly link back to details in the Amara scenario, not just repeat the study generically

practice_questions.text: Evaluate trait theory (Allport, 1936; Cattell, 1946) as an explanation of personality.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sophisticated evaluation that weighs multiple strengths and weaknesses (e.g. scientific measurement vs reductionism, social desirability bias, situational variation) with a supported overall judgement, using accurate detail from both Allport and Cattell.
Secure: Clear evaluation with relevant strengths and weaknesses explained, referring to at least one named theorist, reaching a judgement.
Developing: Some relevant evaluation points made but under-developed or one-sided; limited reference to named theorists.
Emerging: Simple, undeveloped points with little or no reference to Allport or Cattell; no clear judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which part of the neuron releases neurotransmitters into the synapse?
A) The post-synaptic receptor
B) The dendrite
C) Vesicles in the pre-synaptic neuron
D) The cell body
practice_questions.marks: C) Vesicles in the pre-synaptic neuron [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'synapse'.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks:
• The tiny gap between two neurons [1]
• Across which neurotransmitters (chemical messages) pass [1]

practice_questions.text: Explain how a neurotransmitter can cause inhibition in the post-synaptic neuron.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks for a developed explanation, e.g.:
• The neurotransmitter crosses the synapse and binds to receptor sites on the post-synaptic neuron [1]
• This binding decreases the likelihood that the neuron will fire an action potential [1]
• This acts as a 'brake', preventing unwanted signals from spreading through the nervous system [1]

practice_questions.text: Compare the roles of sensory neurons and motor neurons.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Must refer to both neuron types with at least one similarity and one difference, e.g.:
• Similarity: both are specialised nerve cells that transmit information as electrical/chemical signals [1]
• Difference: sensory neurons carry information from sense organs towards the CNS, whereas motor neurons carry instructions from the CNS to muscles/glands [1-2]
• Further difference: sensory neurons respond to stimuli detected by receptors, while motor neurons trigger movement or secretion [1]

practice_questions.text: A student touches a hot pan and pulls their hand away without consciously deciding to do so. Using your knowledge of neurons and synapses, explain how this response occurs.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks for a developed explanation tracing the full pathway, e.g.:
• Sensory neurons detect the heat via receptors in the skin and carry the signal towards the central nervous system (spinal cord) [1-2]
• Relay neurons in the spinal cord process the signal and connect to motor neurons, often as part of a reflex that bypasses conscious brain processing [1-2]
• Motor neurons carry the instruction from the CNS to the muscles in the arm, causing contraction and withdrawal [1-2]
• At each synapse along this pathway, neurotransmitters cross the gap and bind to receptors, causing excitation or inhibition, allowing the signal to pass rapidly between neurons [1-2]

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the usefulness of understanding synaptic transmission for explaining human behaviour.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sophisticated evaluation weighing multiple strengths and weaknesses (e.g. links to real-world treatments like SSRIs, but also the reductionist nature of purely biological explanations), reaching a supported judgement.
Secure: Clear evaluation with at least two developed points (e.g. explains how SSRIs demonstrate the synapse-behaviour link; notes that biological explanations alone may be reductionist).
Developing: Some evaluative comment but underdeveloped or one-sided; may only describe synaptic transmission without evaluating.
Emerging: Basic or unsupported statements with little evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which psychologist proposed the Theory of Reconstructive Memory, tested using the War of the Ghosts story?
A) Peterson and Peterson
B) Bartlett
C) Atkinson and Shiffrin
D) Freud
practice_questions.marks: B) Bartlett [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the story Bartlett used to test his Theory of Reconstructive Memory.
practice_questions.marks: War of the Ghosts [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'schema' as used in Bartlett's Theory of Reconstructive Memory.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying it as a mental framework/structure of knowledge; 1 mark for linking it to past experience being used to interpret or reconstruct new information. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare a reductionist explanation of memory with a holistic explanation of memory.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clearly compares both approaches with a developed similarity and a developed difference, referring to specific memory research (e.g. multi-store model vs Bartlett's theory).
Secure: Identifies at least one similarity and one difference between the approaches, both linked to memory.
Developing: Identifies either a similarity or a difference, with limited development.
Emerging: Vague or one-sided description of reductionism or holism only. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe Bartlett's (1932) War of the Ghosts study, including its aim, procedure, results and conclusion.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for aim (to investigate how memory for an unfamiliar story changes with repeated recall); 1 mark for procedure detail (British participants read an unfamiliar Native American folk tale and recalled it repeatedly over intervals); 1-2 marks for accurate results (story became shorter, more rationalised, unfamiliar details changed or omitted); 1 mark for conclusion (memory is an active reconstruction shaped by schemas, not an exact replay). [5 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'The multi-store model gives a better explanation of memory than Bartlett's Theory of Reconstructive Memory because it is more scientific.' Assess this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sophisticated, balanced assessment weighing the reductionist rigour of the multi-store model against the holistic real-world validity of Bartlett's theory, reaching a clearly supported judgement.
Secure: Clear assessment referencing both theories with developed strengths/weaknesses (e.g. multi-store model's controlled, testable stages vs Bartlett's ecologically valid but poorly controlled study), reaching a judgement.
Developing: Some assessment of one or both theories with limited development; judgement present but under-supported.
Emerging: Simple description of one theory with little or no evaluation or judgement. [9 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which term best describes the loss of personal identity and accountability that can occur when someone is part of a large crowd?
A) Conformity
B) Deindividuation
C) Obedience
D) Social loafing
practice_questions.marks: B) Deindividuation [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'antisocial behaviour' as used in psychology.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying that it is behaviour that harms others or society; one mark for a suitable example (e.g. aggression, vandalism, violence) [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare prosocial and antisocial crowd behaviour.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks for a developed similarity (e.g. both can result from deindividuation reducing personal accountability within a crowd) and up to 2 marks for a developed difference (e.g. prosocial behaviour benefits others, such as collective helping, whereas antisocial behaviour harms others, such as rioting or violence). Full marks require reference to both types of behaviour. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe Haney, Banks and Zimbardo's (1973) study of prisoners and guards in a simulated prison.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content, up to 5 marks:
• Aim: to investigate whether prison brutality was caused by guards' personalities or by the prison situation itself.
• Procedure: student volunteers were randomly assigned to the role of guard or prisoner in a mock prison at Stanford University; guards had uniforms and power, prisoners were addressed only by number.
• Results: guards became abusive, prisoners became distressed and passive, and the study was stopped after six days instead of the planned two weeks.
• Conclusion: the situation and social roles, not personality, caused the brutal and submissive behaviour.
[Award up to 5 marks for accurate, detailed coverage across aim, procedure, results and conclusion]

practice_questions.text: After their team lost an important match, a group of football fans set fire to bins and threw objects at police officers. Using your knowledge of deindividuation, explain why the fans may have behaved this way.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clearly and accurately applies deindividuation to the scenario, explaining how anonymity within the crowd of fans reduced personal accountability and released antisocial behaviour, with sustained, specific reference to the match context throughout.
Secure: Applies deindividuation to the scenario with relevant explanation and some specific reference to the fans and the match context.
Developing: Some explanation of deindividuation is given but application to the scenario is limited or generic.
Emerging: Simple identification of deindividuation with little or no application to the scenario.

practice_questions.text: 'Zimbardo's prison study proves that anyone can become cruel if the situation allows it.' Assess this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Constructs a sustained, well-evidenced assessment that weighs the situational explanation (roles, uniforms, deindividuation) against limitations of the study (small, self-selected male American sample; ethical concerns about protection of participants; possible reduced validity from participants knowing they were observed), reaching a clear, justified overall judgement on how far the statement is supported.
Secure: Assesses the statement with relevant evidence from the study on both sides, reaching a supported conclusion, though development may be less consistent.
Developing: Some relevant points are made about the study's support for or against the statement, but the assessment is one-sided or the conclusion is weak.
Emerging: Simple, undeveloped points about the study with little or no judgement reached.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is an example of negative reinforcement in the learning theory explanation of addiction?
A) Feeling a rush of pleasure after taking a drug
B) Taking a drug to relieve withdrawal symptoms
C) Losing a job because of drug use
D) Refusing a drug when offered by a friend
practice_questions.marks: B) Taking a drug to relieve withdrawal symptoms [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'positive reinforcement' as used in the learning theory explanation of addiction.
practice_questions.marks: Full marks: identifies that a pleasant/rewarding consequence follows a behaviour, and states that this increases the likelihood of the behaviour being repeated. Partial marks: only one of these two elements is present.

practice_questions.text: In a twin study, 9 out of 12 MZ (identical) twin pairs were concordant for addiction, compared with 4 out of 12 DZ (non-identical) twin pairs. Calculate the concordance rate for the MZ twin pairs. Give your answer as a percentage.
practice_questions.marks: 9 ÷ 12 × 100 = 75%. Full marks: correct method/working shown plus the correct final answer of 75% with the % unit included. Partial marks: correct method shown but the final answer is missing, incorrect, or missing the % unit.

practice_questions.text: Compare the genetic explanation of addiction with the learning theory explanation of addiction.
practice_questions.marks: Similarity (1–2 marks) e.g. both explanations attempt to account for why some individuals become addicted while others do not, and both can be evaluated for whether they are deterministic. Difference (1–2 marks) e.g. the genetic explanation is a nature-based explanation, focusing on inherited biological vulnerability tested through twin studies, whereas learning theory is a nurture-based explanation, focusing on reinforcement learned through experience. Full marks require reference to both explanations and at least one similarity and one difference.

practice_questions.text: Priya has started vaping. Every time she feels anxious before an exam, vaping removes her craving and she feels calmer immediately afterwards. Using your knowledge of learning theory, explain how negative reinforcement could account for why Priya continues to vape.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Correctly names negative reinforcement and explains, with sustained reference to Priya, that removing her unpleasant anxious feelings after vaping strengthens the behaviour, making her more likely to vape again in similar situations.
Secure: Names negative reinforcement and explains that removing an unpleasant feeling increases the likelihood of the behaviour being repeated, with some reference to Priya's situation.
Developing: Shows some understanding of reinforcement but the link to Priya's specific scenario is limited, generic or partly inaccurate.
Emerging: Describes vaping or anxiety with little or no reference to negative reinforcement or the scenario.

practice_questions.text: Assess the statement: 'Addiction is caused entirely by a person's genes, not by their environment.'
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sophisticated argument that draws on both the genetic explanation (e.g. twin study evidence of higher MZ concordance) and learning theory (e.g. positive and negative reinforcement) to challenge the statement, and reaches a supported judgement, such as that genetic vulnerability and environmental reinforcement interact.
Secure: Clear argument using evidence and reasoning from both explanations, with a judgement on the statement, though development may be less consistent.
Developing: Some relevant points about genetics and/or learning theory made, but with limited evaluation or a weak/unsupported conclusion.
Emerging: Simple, undeveloped points about addiction; little or no use of named explanations or evidence, and no clear judgement reached.

practice_questions.text:
Which piece of evidence most strongly supports Darwin's claim that non-verbal communication is innate?
A) Yuki et al.'s finding that Japanese participants focus on the eyes
B) Adults learning to use new emoticons on social media
C) Neonates displaying disgust and distress from birth
D) Cultural differences in preferred personal space distance
practice_questions.marks: C) Neonates displaying disgust and distress from birth [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'proxemics'.
practice_questions.marks:
2 marks for a full, accurate definition: the study of the physical distance people keep between themselves and others and what this communicates.
1 mark for a partial definition (e.g. 'to do with personal space' with no reference to study/communication).

practice_questions.text: Compare postural echo with closed posture as forms of body language. Refer to both in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Gives a clear similarity (both are unconscious, non-verbal signals about the relationship between two people) AND a clear difference (postural echo signals rapport/liking, whereas closed posture signals defensiveness/discomfort), referring explicitly to both concepts.
Secure: Gives at least one accurate similarity and one accurate difference, with some reference to both concepts.
Developing: Gives only a similarity or only a difference, or references only one concept in detail.
Emerging: Describes one or both terms without making any comparison.

practice_questions.text: Describe Yuki et al.'s (2007) study into cultural differences in reading emotion from emoticons. Refer to the aim, procedure and findings in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurately describes the aim (investigating cultural differences in judging emotion from emoticons), procedure (Japanese and American participants rated emoticons for happiness/sadness) and findings (Japanese participants focused on the eyes, American participants focused on the mouth), with a brief accurate conclusion.
Secure: Describes most of aim, procedure and findings accurately, with minor omissions or imprecision.
Developing: Describes some correct detail but confuses elements of the study or gives an incomplete procedure/findings.
Emerging: Gives only a vague or inaccurate account of the study.

practice_questions.text: Amaia, who grew up in Japan, is video-calling her new pen pal Ben, who grew up in the United States. Amaia says Ben's smiling emoticon doesn't seem all that happy to her, while Ben says the same about Amaia's emoticon showing 'happy eyes'. Using your knowledge of Yuki et al.'s (2007) research, explain why Amaia and Ben might interpret the same types of emoticons differently.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Applies Yuki et al.'s finding directly to the scenario — explains that Amaia (Japanese) is likely reading eye shape as the main emotional cue while Ben (American) is likely reading mouth shape, so each finds the other's preferred cue less convincing; links this clearly to cultural learning rather than innate biology, using named detail from the study.
Secure: Explains the eyes-versus-mouth difference and applies it reasonably to the scenario, with some development.
Developing: States the general finding (cultural differences exist) without clearly applying it to Amaia and Ben.
Emerging: Describes the scenario without meaningful reference to Yuki et al.'s research.

practice_questions.text: 'Non-verbal communication is entirely innate and cannot be changed by culture.' Assess this statement, using evidence from Darwin's theory and Yuki et al.'s (2007) study.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Considers evidence supporting innateness (Darwin's theory, neonate evidence, sensory-deprived evidence) and evidence against a purely innate view (Yuki et al.'s cross-cultural findings), develops each point with reasoning, and reaches a supported judgement that NVC likely involves both nature and nurture.
Secure: Covers evidence on both sides with some development, reaching a judgement that may be less clearly supported.
Developing: Covers evidence mainly on one side, or lists points on both sides without much development or a clear conclusion.
Emerging: Describes Darwin's theory or Yuki et al.'s study without evaluating the statement or reaching a judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which stage of moral development is typical of a young child who avoids hitting a sibling only because they fear being told off?
A) Post-conventional morality
B) Conventional morality
C) Pre-conventional morality
D) Cognitive development
practice_questions.marks: C) Pre-conventional morality [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'morality' as used in psychology.
practice_questions.marks: A set of principles or standards about what is right and wrong that guide a person's behaviour [1 mark]; used by a person to judge whether an action is right or wrong [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Explain why Willingham argues that practice is important for a student's learning.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that repeated practice makes facts or skills automatic; 1 mark for explaining that this frees up working memory; 1 mark for explaining that the student can then focus on harder problems or tasks instead of basic recall.

practice_questions.text: Compare pre-conventional morality with post-conventional morality.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a valid similarity (e.g. both are stages in the sequence of moral development, and both are used to judge right and wrong). Up to 3 marks for a developed difference referring to both stages (e.g. pre-conventional morality judges behaviour by external reward or punishment, while post-conventional morality judges behaviour by the person's own internalised principles of justice, even when this conflicts with rules or laws).

practice_questions.text: Jamal, aged 16, refuses to copy his friend's homework because he believes cheating is wrong, even though his friend says nobody will find out and he will not be punished. Using your knowledge of the stages of morality, explain which stage of moral development Jamal is showing.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for identifying the correct stage and explaining using detail from the scenario:
• Identifies Jamal's behaviour as post-conventional morality (1-2 marks)
• Explains that Jamal is following his own internal principle about honesty or justice rather than fear of consequences (1-2 marks)
• Links this explicitly to the scenario detail that Jamal will not be caught or punished, showing his morality is not driven by consequences (1-2 marks)
Maximum 6 marks for a full, contextualised explanation.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate Willingham's learning theory as an explanation of how children develop knowledge and skills.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Gives a balanced, detailed evaluation with strengths (e.g. supported by evidence on memory and automatic processing, gives practical strategies for cognitive, physical and social development) and weaknesses (e.g. may underestimate innate ability, motivation or creativity, difficult to test scientifically) and reaches a supported overall judgement.
Secure: Gives clear strengths and weaknesses of the theory with some development, and attempts a conclusion.
Developing: Identifies some strengths or weaknesses but with limited explanation or development; conclusion may be missing or weak.
Emerging: Simple, undeveloped points about the theory with little or no evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes prosopagnosia?
A) An inability to recognise any objects due to poor eyesight
B) An inability to recognise faces despite normal vision and intelligence
C) A loss of speech following brain damage
D) An inability to control impulses after frontal lobe damage
practice_questions.marks: B) An inability to recognise faces despite normal vision and intelligence [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'pre-frontal cortex'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying it as the front part of the frontal lobe; 1 mark for stating its role in decision-making, planning, impulse control or personality regulation. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare visual agnosia and prosopagnosia.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 4 marks: 1-2 marks for a valid similarity (e.g. both involve normal eyesight but an inability to recognise what is seen; both result from damage to visual processing areas of the brain). 1-2 marks for a valid difference (e.g. visual agnosia affects recognition of objects in general, whereas prosopagnosia is limited specifically to faces). Answer must refer to both conditions. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the aim, procedure and findings of Damasio et al. (1994) 'The Return of Phineas Gage'.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Accurately describes aim, procedure and findings/conclusion of the correct study with precise detail (e.g. neuroimaging reconstruction of the skull, damage confined to the pre-frontal cortex, personality change without loss of intelligence). Secure: Describes most of aim, procedure and findings with minor gaps or imprecision. Developing: Describes some elements of the study but is vague, muddled or omits a key stage. Emerging: Very limited or inaccurate reference to the study; may confuse it with another named study. [5 marks]

practice_questions.text: A woman survives a car accident that damages the front part of her frontal lobe. Her family say she can still talk, walk and remember things normally, but she has become impulsive and makes poor decisions she would never have made before. Using your knowledge of the pre-frontal cortex and the Phineas Gage case, explain why this pattern of symptoms has occurred.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 6 marks: 2 marks for identifying the pre-frontal cortex as the damaged area and linking it to decision-making, impulse control or personality regulation. 2 marks for reasoned explanation of why intelligence, speech and memory are unaffected (these functions are localised elsewhere in the brain). 2 marks for explicit reference to the scenario details and/or a valid comparison with Phineas Gage's case. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Studying rare, unusual cases like Phineas Gage tells psychologists very little about how the normal brain works.' Assess this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated, balanced assessment considering strengths (unique real-world evidence of cause and effect, cannot be ethically created in a lab, supported by later scientific evidence such as Damasio's reconstruction) and weaknesses (single case, historical reliability of witness reports, limited generalisability) with a clear, justified conclusion. Secure: Clear assessment covering both strengths and weaknesses with some development, reaching a conclusion. Developing: Some relevant points made but one-sided, underdeveloped or lacking a clear conclusion. Emerging: Simple, undeveloped assertion with little reasoning or evidence. [9 marks]

before.exam_tip_html: For “Describe a Study” questions on Damasio et al., structure your answer around aim, procedure, results and conclusion in that order — examiners reward this clear structure specifically. For “Assess” or “Evaluate” items on this study, always pair a strength with a weakness and develop each with a reason (for example, “this is a weakness because…”), then finish with a supported judgement rather than just listing points.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes validity?
A) Getting the same results every time a study is repeated
B) Measuring what the study claims to measure
C) Selecting a sample using a computer-generated list
D) Debriefing participants after a study has ended
practice_questions.marks: B) Measuring what the study claims to measure [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State one ethical issue that a researcher must deal with when running a study that does not tell participants its true purpose.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for a correct issue, e.g. deception [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'right to withdraw' as used in psychological research.
practice_questions.marks: The entitlement of a participant to stop taking part in a study at any point, and to withdraw their data afterwards, without giving a reason or facing a penalty. [2 marks for a full, accurate definition; 1 mark for a partial definition]

practice_questions.text: Compare the reliability and validity of quantitative data with qualitative data.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks for at least one similarity and one difference, referring to both types of data:
• Similarity: Both can be affected by how a researcher chooses to interpret or record data.
• Difference: Quantitative data (numbers) is usually easier to check for reliability by direct repetition; qualitative data (words) is harder to check for reliability because different researchers may interpret it differently.
• Difference: Qualitative data often captures more depth and can support validity; quantitative data can miss the depth of an experience.
Mastering: sustained comparison with a developed similarity and difference referring to both types. Secure: at least one similarity and one difference, both referred to. Developing: one-sided comparison or brief undeveloped points. Emerging: vague or single unexplained point.

practice_questions.text: A researcher studies obedience by secretly observing how commuters react when a stranger asks them to give up their seat on a train, without telling them beforehand that they are part of a study. Explain two ethical issues raised by this study and how the researcher could deal with each one.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks per ethical issue (2 issues x 3 marks):
• Identify a relevant issue, e.g. lack of informed consent / use of deception / difficulty protecting participants from embarrassment.
• Explain why it applies to this specific scenario (commuters did not know and could not agree in advance).
• State a practical way of dealing with it, e.g. debriefing commuters afterwards and giving them the right to withdraw their data.
Mastering: both issues explained with context and a workable solution. Secure: two issues identified with explanation but weaker solutions. Developing: one issue explained fully, or two issues named with limited explanation. Emerging: issues named only, with no explanation or context.

practice_questions.text: 'Ethical guidelines make it impossible to conduct valuable psychological research.' Assess this statement, using examples from named studies you have studied.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A well-supported, balanced assessment using at least two named studies (e.g. Piliavin et al.'s use of deception in a field study to gain naturalistic data; Zimbardo's simulated prison study, which was stopped early to protect participants). Considers both that ethics can restrict what is possible (e.g. limiting field experiments and deception) and that ethical safeguards (debriefing, right to withdraw) allow valuable research to still take place safely. Ends with a clear, supported judgement.
Secure: A clear assessment using at least one named study, with some balance between both sides of the argument and a judgement, though less developed.
Developing: Some relevant points made about ethics and research value, but with limited use of named studies or an unbalanced argument.
Emerging: Simple, undeveloped points about ethics or research with little reference to studies and no clear judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is a drug treatment that increases the availability of serotonin at the synapse to relieve symptoms of depression?
A) CBT-IA
B) SSRI antidepressant
C) Nicotine replacement therapy
D) Harm reduction therapy
practice_questions.marks: B) SSRI antidepressant [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'nurture' as used in the nature-nurture debate.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: Nurture refers to the influence of environment, experience or upbringing on behaviour.
1 mark: This is contrasted with nature (innate, inherited/genetic factors). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how CBT-IA might help someone reduce an internet addiction.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains at least two stages of CBT-IA (e.g. behaviour modification and cognitive restructuring) with clear reasoning linking each to reduced internet use.
Secure: Explains at least one stage of CBT-IA with clear reasoning.
Developing: Describes a stage of CBT-IA without clear reasoning/justification.
Emerging: Vague or inaccurate reference to CBT with little explanation.

practice_questions.text: Compare drug treatment and CBT as ways of treating addiction.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Gives one clear similarity and one clear difference, referring explicitly to both drug treatment and CBT, each point developed.
Secure: Gives one similarity and one difference referring to both treatments, with adequate development.
Developing: Gives only a similarity or only a difference, or refers to just one treatment.
Emerging: Vague or inaccurate comparison with minimal reference to either treatment.

practice_questions.text: Describe Young's (2007) study into cognitive behaviour therapy with internet addicts, including the aim, procedure, results and conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Gives an accurate aim, procedure, results and conclusion of Young's (2007) study, referring to the structured course of CBT sessions with internet-addicted clients and outcomes assessed at the end of treatment and at follow-up, using precise psychological language throughout.
Secure: Gives most of the aim, procedure, results and conclusion accurately, with minor gaps or imprecise use of terminology.
Developing: Gives a general description of the study with at least two of the four elements (aim/procedure/results/conclusion) present.
Emerging: Gives a vague or partial description with little accurate detail of the study.

practice_questions.text: 'Nature is more important than nurture in explaining why people develop addictions.' Assess this statement, using your knowledge of explanations and treatments for addiction.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sophisticated argument drawing on genetic (nature) and learning/cognitive (nurture) explanations and treatment evidence (e.g. Young, 2007) to reach a well-supported, balanced judgement.
Secure: Clear argument considering both nature and nurture, using relevant explanations and at least one treatment or study as evidence, reaching a supported judgement.
Developing: Some discussion of nature and/or nurture with limited use of evidence; judgement may be one-sided or underdeveloped.
Emerging: Simple, undeveloped points about nature or nurture with little or no supporting evidence or judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which measure of central tendency is most affected by a single extreme outlier?
A) Mode
B) Median
C) Mean
D) All three are affected equally
practice_questions.marks: C) Mean [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'secondary data'.
practice_questions.marks: Full marks (2): definition captures both elements — that secondary data was collected by someone else, often for a different purpose, and that it is being reused by the current researcher. Partial marks (1): definition includes only one of these two elements. No marks: definition is inaccurate or describes primary data instead.

practice_questions.text: A psychologist tests six participants' reaction times, in seconds: 0.4, 0.6, 0.5, 0.9, 0.5, 0.3. Calculate the mean reaction time, showing your working.
practice_questions.marks: Full marks (2): correct working shown (0.4 + 0.6 + 0.5 + 0.9 + 0.5 + 0.3 = 3.2, divided by 6) leading to the correct answer with unit, approximately 0.53 seconds. Partial marks (1): correct working shown but the final answer is missing, incorrect, or lacks a unit. No marks: no working shown and an incorrect answer.

practice_questions.text: Compare quantitative data and qualitative data as used in psychological research.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Gives at least one accurate similarity and one accurate difference, referring to both quantitative and qualitative data, each point developed with an example or reason.
Secure: Gives one similarity and one difference referring to both data types, with some development.
Developing: Gives only a similarity or only a difference, or both but undeveloped and lacking reference to both types.
Emerging: Vague, inaccurate or one-sided comparison with no clear similarity or difference.

practice_questions.text: A researcher surveys 40 students about hours of sleep per night and records their exam scores. She wants to display the relationship between the two variables. Explain how she should display this data and what the resulting pattern would tell her.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Names the scatter diagram, explains that each point represents one participant's pair of scores, and explains what a positive, negative and zero correlation pattern would each indicate about the sleep-exam score relationship.
Secure: Names the scatter diagram and gives a partial explanation of what an upward or downward pattern would show.
Developing: Identifies a suitable graph but gives limited explanation of what patterns mean.
Emerging: Names an unsuitable display method or gives no explanation of the pattern.

practice_questions.text: 'The mean is always the best measure of central tendency to use when analysing psychological data.' Assess this statement, using your knowledge of mean, median and mode.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Gives a balanced assessment covering strengths of the mean (uses all data, most sensitive) and weaknesses (distorted by outliers), compares to median and mode with developed reasoning, and reaches a supported judgement about when each is most appropriate.
Secure: Discusses at least two of the three measures with some development and reaches a conclusion, though reasoning may be less developed.
Developing: Describes the three measures with limited evaluation and a weak or unsupported conclusion.
Emerging: Describes one or two measures with little or no evaluation and no conclusion.
